tasks.q: Why do computers need secondary storage?
a: To keep programs and data permanently, even when the power is off
Because the CPU works from it directly
Because it is faster than RAM
tasks.fb: Non-volatile storage is what makes saving possible.

a: Secondary storage is slower than RAM but much larger and cheaper per gigabyte
Secondary storage is faster than RAM
tasks.fb: That trade-off is why computers have both.

tasks.q: How does a hard disk drive store data?
a: By magnetising tiny areas on spinning platters
By burning pits with a laser
In flash memory cells with no moving parts
tasks.fb: The read/write head floats just above the surface.

tasks.q: What is magnetic tape mostly used for now?
a: Large, cheap, long-term backups and archives
tasks.fb: Tape is slow to search but very cheap per terabyte.

tasks.q: How is data read from an optical disc?
a: A laser detects pits and lands on the surface
Electricity is trapped in flash cells
tasks.fb: Blu-ray uses a blue laser with a shorter wavelength, so it fits more data.

tasks.q: Put these optical discs in order of capacity, smallest first.
tasks.fb: Each generation uses a shorter-wavelength laser.

tasks.q: How does solid state storage hold data?
a: As electrical charge in flash memory cells, with no moving parts
As pits burned by a laser
tasks.fb: No moving parts means it's quiet, fast and hard to damage by knocks.

tasks.q: Which is a disadvantage of solid state storage?
a: It costs more per gigabyte than magnetic storage
It is easily damaged by being dropped
tasks.fb: Prices keep falling, but magnetic is still cheaper per terabyte.

tasks.q: Match each part to the type of storage it belongs to.
pairs: Spinning platters and a read/write head
A laser reading pits and lands
Flash memory chips and a controller
A long spool read in sequence
tasks.fb: Knowing how each works explains its strengths and weaknesses.

tasks.q: A laptop needs fast, durable storage for its operating system. Which type?
tasks.fb: SSDs boot quickly and survive being carried around.

tasks.q: A company needs to archive 500 TB cheaply, and rarely needs it back. Which type?
tasks.fb: Tape is the cheapest way to store enormous archives.

info.title: The first hard disk
info.text: IBM's first hard disk, in 1956, stored about 3.75 MB, weighed over a tonne and was delivered by forklift.

info.title: Heads that fly
info.text: A hard disk's head floats just nanometres above the platter, closer than a speck of dust. That's why a knock can wreck it.

info.title: Why Blu-ray?
info.text: A blue laser has a shorter wavelength than a red one, so it can read smaller pits, which means more data on the same-sized disc.

info.title: Tape lives on
info.text: Tape is far from dead: it stores much of the world's long-term archives, including film studios' back catalogues.

info.title: Wear levelling
info.text: Flash cells wear out after many writes, so SSD controllers spread writes evenly across the chips to make them last.

info.title: M-DISC
info.text: Some archival optical discs claim a lifespan of hundreds of years, far longer than a typical hard drive.
